root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Fix any integer n with n > 1. Define f_n(x) = floor(n x) - sum from k=1 to n of (floor(k x) divided by k). Determine the real number(s) x where f_n(x) attains its maximum over all real x, and give the corresponding maximum value.
quantifier_order: for each integer n with n > 1
choose real x to maximize the expression over all real x

payload.theorem_nl: Let $n$ be an integer greater than 1. For which real numbers $x$ is \\[\\lfloor nx \\rfloor - \\sum_{k=1}^{n} \\frac{\\lfloor kx \\rfloor}{k}\\] maximal, and what is the maximal value that this expression can take?

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Use 1-periodicity to reduce an arbitrary real x to y = frac(x) in [0,1). Then choose m = floor(n y), so y lies in the interval [m/n,(m+1)/n). On that interval the function is nonincreasing, hence F_n(y) is at most the left endpoint value F_n(m/n). Evaluate that endpoint explicitly as a discrete floor-sum, and apply the hard discrete inequality to bound it by H_n - 1, with equality only when m = n-1. Finally, on the last interval [(n-1)/n,1) every floor(kx) equals k-1, so the value there is exactly H_n - 1. Therefore the maximum is H_n - 1 and the maximizers are exactly the integers translates of that last interval, equivalently the real x with frac(x) in [(n-1)/n,1).

steps.derives: For an arbitrary real x, replace x by its fractional part y = frac(x) = x - floor(x); then F_n(x) = F_n(y), and y lies in [0,1).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply the periodicity lemma with z = floor(x), which is an integer, and note that x - floor(x) = frac(x).

steps.derives: Let y = frac(x), and let m = floor(n y). Then 0 <= m <= n-1 and y lies in [m/n,(m+1)/n), so F_n(y) <= F_n(m/n).
steps.trivial_justification: This uses the floor characterization of the interval index m together with the interval monotonicity lemma: once y is placed in the correct half-open interval, the value at y is bounded above by the left endpoint m/n.

steps.derives: Rewrite the endpoint value as F_n(m/n) = m - sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(k m/n)/k.
steps.trivial_justification: This is a direct substitution of x = m/n into the definition of F_n.

steps.derives: Conclude F_n(y) <= H_n - 1, with equality only if m = n-1.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the discrete comparison lemma applied to the endpoint expression from the previous step.

steps.derives: Every real x with frac(x) in [(n-1)/n,1) satisfies F_n(x) = H_n - 1; equivalently, every integer translate of the interval [(n-1)/n,1) is a maximizer set.
steps.trivial_justification: The last interval forces every floor(kx) to equal k-1, so the expression evaluates immediately to H_n - 1.

steps.derives: The maximal value of floor(n x) - sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(k x)/k over all real x is H_n - 1 = sum_{k=2}^{n} 1/k, and the maximizers are exactly the real numbers x with frac(x) in [(n-1)/n,1), equivalently x in the union over z in Z of [z + (n-1)/n, z + 1).
steps.trivial_justification: Steps A1-A4 give a universal upper bound H_n - 1 for every real x, while A5 shows that this bound is attained precisely on the stated periodic family of intervals. Combining the upper bound with the attainment description yields both the maximal value and the exact maximizer set.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Reduce the maximization problem to x in [0,1) by replacing x with its fractional part.
lemmas.self_check_notes: Only uses the standard floor translation rule and cancellation of integer shifts.

domain_restrictions: n is an integer with n > 1
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: The expression defining F_n is 1-periodic because floor(t+z)=floor(t)+z for integer z, and the added linear terms cancel.
quantifier_order: for all real x and all integers z

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n be an integer greater than 1, and define F_n(x) = floor(n x) - sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(k x)/k. Then for every real x and every integer z, F_n(x + z) = F_n(x).
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: This is a direct floor-identity calculation: each floor(k(x+z)) = floor(kx) + k z, so the numerator and denominator terms cancel after summation.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Show that, on each interval [m/n,(m+1)/n), the maximum occurs at the left endpoint m/n.
lemmas.self_check_notes: The statement is local and uses only monotonicity of floor together with the interval where floor(n x) does not change.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: On each half-open interval I_m = [m/n,(m+1)/n), the function x -> F_n(x) is nonincreasing because floor(n x) is constant there and each floor(k x) is nondecreasing in x.
quantifier_order: for each integer m with 0 <= m <= n-1
witness_dependencies: the interval endpoint m is the common value of floor(n t) for t in [m/n,(m+1)/n)

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n be an integer greater than 1, and define F_n(x) = floor(n x) - sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(k x)/k. For any integer m with 0 <= m <= n-1 and any real numbers x,y satisfying m/n <= x <= y < (m+1)/n, one has F_n(x) >= F_n(y).
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: This is a local monotonicity statement: floor(n x) is constant on the interval, while each floor(k x) is monotone nondecreasing, so the difference is monotone nonincreasing.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Convert the endpoint value into the discrete floor-sum expression to which the hard inequality applies.
lemmas.self_check_notes: No hidden structure: it is a one-line evaluation of the defining formula at x = m/n.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: At the rational point x = m/n, the top floor term floor(n x) equals m, so the value of F_n is the explicit discrete floor-sum at m/n.
quantifier_order: for each integer m with 0 <= m <= n-1
witness_dependencies: substitute x = m/n directly into the defining formula for F_n

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n be an integer greater than 1, and define F_n(x) = floor(n x) - sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(k x)/k. For every integer m with 0 <= m <= n-1, F_n(m/n) = m - sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(k m/n)/k.
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: This is just direct substitution into the definition of F_n and the identity floor(n * m/n) = m.

lemmas.bottleneck_reason: After periodic reduction and interval monotonicity, the theorem reduces to comparing finitely many rational endpoints. Proving that every endpoint value is at most H_n - 1, with equality only at m = n-1, is the hard arithmetic/combinatorial floor-sum inequality that controls the entire optimization problem.
lemmas.role_in_assembly: This is the main discrete comparison step that identifies the global maximum among the rational endpoints.
lemmas.self_check_notes: This is the only genuinely difficult floor-sum estimate; the rest of the decomposition is routine periodicity and monotonicity.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Among all rational endpoints x = m/n, the corresponding value of F_n is at most H_n - 1, and the unique equality case occurs at the last endpoint m = n-1.
quantifier_order: for each integer m with 0 <= m <= n-1
witness_dependencies: the equality witness is m = n-1

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n be an integer greater than 1, and define H_n = sum_{k=1}^{n} 1/k. For every integer m with 0 <= m <= n-1, m - sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(k m/n)/k <= H_n - 1, and equality holds if and only if m = n-1.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Show that the upper bound from the discrete comparison is actually attained on the last interval, giving the full maximizing set.
lemmas.self_check_notes: This is a direct evaluation on the last interval after reducing modulo 1.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: On the final fractional interval, every term floor(kx) reaches its maximal value k-1, so the expression evaluates to H_n - 1.
witness_dependencies: for 1 <= k <= n, all floors floor(k * frac(x)) equal k - 1

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n be an integer greater than 1, define F_n(x) = floor(n x) - sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(k x)/k, and define frac(x) = x - floor(x). If frac(x) lies in the interval [(n-1)/n, 1), then F_n(x) = H_n - 1, where H_n = sum_{k=1}^{n} 1/k.
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: Once the fractional part is in the final interval, each floor(kx) is forced to be k-1 for 1 <= k <= n, so the value is immediate.

candidates.strategy_summary: Reduce the problem modulo 1, then use the partition of [0,1) into the intervals [m/n,(m+1)/n). On each interval the function is nonincreasing, so the maximum there occurs at the left endpoint m/n. The only hard step is a discrete floor-sum inequality at those rational endpoints, which shows the unique global maximizers come from the last interval [ (n-1)/n, 1 ) modulo integers.
